sentences.text: In the summer of seventeen fifty-two, a grown man walked out into a thunderstorm and flew a kite into the clouds, on purpose.
Why would anyone do that?
And why does almost every tall building you have ever seen still carry the answer on its roof?
By the end of this film, you'll know how a kite, a key and a glass jar proved what lightning really is, and how one simple idea stopped it burning our towns down.
For thousands of years, lightning was a mystery.
It fell without warning, split trees, killed animals in the fields and set roofs alight.
Many people believed it was a punishment sent from the heavens.
Picture yourself in a town in those years, on a hot summer night.
You would see the sky flash white, hear the thunder crack right overhead, and smell the smoke as a barn went up in flames.
And you could do nothing but wait for the next strike.
The tallest buildings were hit most of all.
Church steeples were struck again and again.
And when a storm came, the bell-ringers were sent up the tower to ring the bells, because people believed the sound would drive the lightning away.
It was the worst place to stand.
One eighteenth-century count found more than a hundred bell-ringers killed by lightning in just a few decades.
So what was lightning?
A punishment?
A kind of fire?
Or something else, something you could catch and study?
In the seventeen-forties, electricity was a party trick.
Travelling lecturers rubbed glass tubes with silk and made sparks fly from people's fingers and hair.
Audiences paid to feel the shock.
In Philadelphia, a printer called Benjamin Franklin saw one of these shows, and could not stop thinking about it.
He was so curious that he handed his printing business to a partner, so he would have time to study electricity.
His most exciting tool was a new invention called a Leyden jar.
It was a glass jar lined with metal foil, and it could store electricity, then let it all go at once, in a bright spark with a loud crack.
And that spark reminded Franklin of something.
A flash of light.
A crack of noise.
A sharp smell in the air.
It was like a tiny thunderstorm in a jar.
So in November seventeen forty-nine, he wrote a list in his notebook.
Twelve ways a spark was just like lightning.
They both gave light of the same colour.
They both moved in crooked lines.
They both made a crack, set things on fire and could kill animals.
But a list of likenesses isn't proof.
At the bottom of the page, Franklin wrote five famous words.
Let the experiment be made.
But how do you catch a bolt of lightning, without it killing you?
Franklin had a plan.
Points, he had found, were very good at drawing electricity out of the air.
So he proposed putting a tall iron rod, sharp at the tip, on top of a high tower.
If lightning really was electricity, the rod should pull sparks out of a passing storm cloud.
He published the idea, and it crossed the ocean.
In May seventeen fifty-two, in a garden at Marly, near Paris, French scientists put up a tall pointed rod and tried it.
As a storm cloud passed, sparks jumped from the rod.
It worked.
But Franklin didn't know yet.
News took weeks to cross the Atlantic.
And Philadelphia had no tower tall enough.
So, about a month later, he had another idea.
A kite could fly higher than any steeple.
He made one from a silk handkerchief and two crossed sticks of cedar, so it would survive the rain.
On top he fixed a sharp wire.
The string was ordinary twine, and near his hand he tied an iron key, then a ribbon of silk to hold it by.
The silk was the clever part.
Wet twine would carry electricity, but dry silk would not.
So Franklin stood inside a shed, out of the rain, and kept the ribbon dry.
He told almost no one.
He was afraid people would laugh if it failed.
Only his son William, a young man of about twenty-one, came along to help.
William ran across the field and the kite climbed into the dark clouds.
Then they waited.
Imagine standing in that doorway, the storm overhead, holding a string that runs up into the sky.
What would you feel, waiting for something to happen?
For a long time, nothing did.
Then Franklin noticed the loose threads of the twine.
They were standing up on end, and pushing away from each other.
Slowly, Franklin brought his knuckle close to the key.
A spark jumped across, with a tiny snap.
Exactly the kind of spark he had made a thousand times in his own room.
Then he touched the key to his Leyden jar, and filled it, with electricity from the sky.
It behaved in every way like the electricity he made with glass and silk.
Lightning and the spark in the jar were the same thing.
Electricity.
And here is the part that most people get wrong.
The kite was never struck by lightning.
If it had been, Franklin would almost certainly have died.
Instead, the kite gathered a little of the storm's electric charge, which ran quietly down the wet string to the key.
It was still dangerous.
The next summer, a scientist in Russia called Georg Richmann was trying a similar experiment with a rod during a storm, and he was killed.
Franklin had been careful, and lucky.
In October, Franklin published how to do the kite experiment in his own newspaper.
His letters were read at the Royal Society in London, and the next year it gave him its highest award, the Copley Medal.
But Franklin wasn't only interested in proving an idea.
He wanted to use it.
If a pointed rod could pull electricity from the sky, could it also keep lightning away from people's homes?
In September seventeen fifty-two, Franklin put an iron rod on top of his own house.
He ran a wire from it into the house and hung two little bells by the stairs.
Whenever a storm cloud passed overhead, the bells rang on their own.
Then he told everyone how to protect their homes.
In his popular yearly almanac, Poor Richard, he printed simple instructions.
Fix an iron rod up the outside wall, with a sharp point high above the roof, and the other end buried deep in damp ground.
Here's how it works.
Lightning is a giant spark, hotter than the surface of the Sun.
It's looking for the easiest path to the ground.
A wooden roof or a stone steeple is a terrible path, so it bursts into flame or cracks apart.
But a metal rod is an easy path.
So the lightning takes the rod, round the outside of the building, and goes harmlessly into the earth.
Franklin never patented his lightning rod.
He wanted everyone to have it.
Within a few years, rods were going up on churches, houses and ships' masts.
And one by one, church towers became safer places to stand.
Why was this so groundbreaking?
Because it was one of the very first times an idea from a laboratory reached out and protected ordinary people from one of nature's deadliest forces.
It showed that the wild things in the sky follow rules, and that once you understand the rules, you can stay safe.
So next time a storm rolls in, look up at the tallest building you can see.
There's a good chance you'll spot a thin metal rod at the very top.
Some tall towers are struck by lightning more than twenty times in a single year, and stay standing.
A kite, a key and a jar.
Together, they took lightning out of the realm of mystery, and put a little piece of it on every roof.
Long before Franklin, a young man in an English garden asked a different question about the sky.
If an apple falls to the ground, why doesn't the Moon?
